chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from al-Hasan al-Lu'lu'i from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Musaddif who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): Does a woman perform Hajj on behalf of a man? He said: Yes, if she is a jurist (faqihah), a Muslim, and she has already performed Hajj. For indeed, there are women who are better than men. So he stipulated for the validity of her Hajj on his behalf the combination of the two conditions: knowledge of the rituals of Hajj, and that she has already performed Hajj. Thus, both must be considered together, and this is further confirmed.

key_terms.فَقِيهَةً: A female jurist or one possessing deep religious knowledge
key_terms.مَنَاسِكِ الْحَجِّ: The rituals and rites of Hajj

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a woman to perform Hajj on behalf of a man in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Al-Istibsar*, Shaykh al-Tusi records Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) ruling that a woman may perform Hajj on behalf of a man, contingent upon her being a *faqihah* (knowledgeable in rituals) and having already fulfilled her own obligatory Hajj. This dual condition underscores the Shia emphasis on both ritual competence and the prior discharge of personal duty, reflecting the principle that a substitute must be spiritually and practically qualified. The narration highlights the flexibility within Shia jurisprudence regarding gender roles in religious obligations, provided the requisite scholarly and spiritual standards are met.
